1.title: MCP Servers and Agentic Customization
1.text: Welcome to Module twelve: M C P Servers and Agentic Customization. This module covers the skills m c p server development, agentic customization. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things. The Model Context Protocol (M C P): client and server roles, and the three server primitives. Authoring an M C P (Model Context Protocol) server, transports (stdio, H T T P), logging rules, deployment and integration. Agentic customization: choosing among built-in tools, custom tools, Skills and M C P.

1.title: Case Check-In: Tidewater Shares Its Policy System
1.text: Our running case is Tidewater Insurance. Tidewater Shares Its Policy System. Three Claude applications need the same policy lookup: the claims assistant, a Claude Code workflow for engineers, and an Agent S D K (software development kit) back-office agent. The policy team wants to maintain the integration in one place.

1.title: MCP Server Development
1.text: M C P Server Development. The figure shows this: M C P: the host's client connects to servers; each server exposes tools, resources and prompts for an external system.

1.title: MCP Server Development, continued
1.text: M C P Server Development, continued. Tools. What it is: Functions the model can call (with user or host approval). Example: get policy, create payment request. Resources. What it is: File-like data that clients can read. Example: A policy P D F, a schema, an A P I (application programming interface) response. Prompts. What it is: Pre-written templates that help users do a task. Example: "Review a claim" template. Roles: the host (the application) runs an M C P client that connects to M C P servers. A server wraps an external system once, and any M C P-capable application can use it.

1.title: MCP Server Development, continued
1.text: M C P Server Development, continued. Authoring: use an official S D K (for example Python or Type Script); tool definitions can be generated from type hints and docstrings (a decorator such as @mcp.tool()); then run the server with a transport.

1.title: MCP Server Development, continued
1.text: M C P Server Development, continued. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Transports and logging
1.text: Transports and logging. stdio. How it works: The client launches the server as a local subprocess and exchanges Jason (Java Script Object Notation)-R P C messages over stdin and stdout. Use for: Local tools for one user or machine. H T T P (streamable H T T P). How it works: The server runs as a network service; clients connect over H T T P. Use for: Remote, shared, independently deployed servers. Never write to stdout in a stdio server. Standard output carries the protocol messages, so a stray print() corrupts them and breaks the server. Log to stderr (or a file) with a logging library.

1.title: Transports and logging, continued
1.text: Transports and logging, continued. The figure shows this: In a stdio M C P server, stdout belongs to the protocol: log to stderr.

1.title: Deploying and integrating
1.text: Deploying and integrating. Claude Code: add servers in project dot M C P dot Jason (shared) or user configuration, with credentials from environment variables; local servers use stdio, remote ones H T T P. Your own applications: use an M C P client library or the platform's M C P support to discover the server's tools and pass them to the model. Share and maintain once: a server fixes the integration problem for many applications; version it and test its tools like any A P I. Exam tip: A capability needed by several Claude applications and maintained independently is an M C P server. A print() in a stdio server breaks it: log to stderr. Exam tip: Ask what is missing: access (tool or M C P), a procedure (Skill) or a common operation (built-in tool).

1.title: Agentic Customization: Which Mechanism?
1.text: Agentic Customization: Which Mechanism? The figure shows this: Choose the extension mechanism: built-in tools for common operations, custom tools for one app, Skills for procedures, M C P for shared external capabilities.

1.title: Agentic Customization: Which Mechanism?, continued
1.text: Agentic Customization: Which Mechanism?, continued. Built-in tools. What it is: Provided by the platform (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob, web tools). Choose it when: The need is common: files, shell, search, web. Trade-off: Nothing to build; limited to what is provided. Custom tools. What it is: Functions you define and run in one application. Choose it when: App-specific logic with tight control. Trade-off: You build, test and run them; not reusable elsewhere. Skills. What it is: Folders with instructions, and optional scripts and resources, loaded on demand. Choose it when: Procedures and expertise (a review checklist, a report format, a workflow). Trade-off: Teaches how, does not give new access; progressive loading keeps context small.

1.title: Agentic Customization: Which Mechanism?, continued
1.text: Agentic Customization: Which Mechanism?, continued. M C P servers. What it is: Shared, independently maintained servers exposing tools, resources and prompts. Choose it when: A capability many applications need, or an external system to integrate. Trade-off: More to deploy and secure; extra connection and tool-definition context.

1.title: How Skills load (progressive disclosure)
1.text: How Skills load (progressive disclosure). Metadata (name and description) is always loaded so Claude knows the Skill exists and when to use it. The instructions (Skill dot M D body) are loaded when the Skill is triggered. Resources and scripts are loaded only as needed; scripts run through the shell, so their code does not enter the context.

1.title: How Skills load (progressive disclosure), continued
1.text: How Skills load (progressive disclosure), continued. The figure shows this: Skills load in stages: metadata first, instructions when triggered, resources and scripts only as needed. Combine them: an M C P server gives access, a Skill gives the procedure for using it well, and built-in tools cover the common steps. Exam tip: Ask what is missing: access to a system (tool or M C P), knowledge of a procedure (Skill), or a common operation (built-in tool). Pick the mechanism that supplies exactly that.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. M C P roles: Host with M C P client and M C P server. Primitives: Tools (functions), resources (readable data), prompts (templates). Authoring: Official S D K s; tools from type hints and docstrings; mcp.run(transport equals "stdio"). Transports: stdio (local subprocess, Jason-R P C on stdin or stdout), H T T P (remote service). Logging: Never stdout in stdio servers; log to stderr. Integrate: dot M C P dot Jason (project) or user config; credentials from env vars. Choose: Built-in equals common ops, custom tool equals one app, Skill equals procedure, M C P equals shared external capability. Skills: Metadata always, Skill dot M D when triggered, resources and scripts as needed.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Three Claude applications need the same internal H R lookup, maintained by the H R team independently. What fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. M C P gives a reusable integration that the H R team can maintain independently for every application.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. An M C P stdio server stops working after a developer adds print("debug") statements. Why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Stdio servers must keep stdout for protocol messages and log to stderr.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Which are the three primitives an M C P server can expose? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Servers expose tools (functions), resources (readable data) and prompts (templates).

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A team needs Claude to follow its claim-review checklist and output format every time it is relevant, with no new system access. What fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Skills teach procedures and expertise on demand; they do not add access.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. What does progressive disclosure mean for Skills? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Staged loading keeps the context small until a Skill is needed.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A function is needed by one application only and must run entirely in that application's code. Which mechanism fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. App-specific logic belongs in a custom tool unless reuse justifies a server.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. Select two. Which two statements about M C P transports are correct? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and D. Local servers use stdio and remote ones use H T T P; stdio logs belong on stderr.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all seven answers. Question one: C. Question two: D. Question three: B. Question four: C. Question five: D. Question six: B. Question seven: A and D. In the next module, we continue the course.
